title: React Components, JSX and Lists: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes for React function components, JSX rules, keyed lists, conditional rendering, children composition and fragments. Ordered from mental model to common mistakes, ending with a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Components and JSX Mental Model
points: A function component is a plain function that takes props and returns JSX; its name must start with a capital letter or React treats it as an HTML tag
UI = f(props, state): rendering must be pure, so the same inputs give the same output and no side effects run in the body
JSX is syntax sugar for createElement/jsx calls that return plain element objects, not DOM nodes
Props are read-only: never mutate props, and pass changing data down as new values
Each render call is a fresh snapshot: React re-calls the function when props or state change and diffs the result

chapters.title: JSX Rules and Core Workflow
points: A component returns a single root: wrap siblings in a parent element or a fragment
Every tag must be closed, including self-closing ones like and
Use camelCase attributes: className, htmlFor, onClick, tabIndex; style takes an object: style={{ color: 'red' }}
{} embeds any JavaScript expression (variables, calls, ternaries) but not statements like if or for
Strings in quotes are static, {} values are dynamic: <Avatar size={40} name="Ada" /> passes a number and a string
Workflow: define the component, destructure props in the signature, return JSX, then render it as <Name prop={value} />

chapters.title: Lists, Keys and Conditional Rendering
points: Render lists with items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} {...} />); the key goes on the outermost element returned inside map
Keys must be stable and unique among siblings: use a database id, not Math.random() and not the array index for lists that reorder, insert or delete
Index keys cause state to attach to the wrong row after reordering because React matches by key
Ternary cond ? <A /> : <B /> picks one of two; && renders only when true; return null renders nothing
Gotcha: {count && <Badge />} renders the number 0 when count is 0; use count > 0 && ... instead
Early return pattern: if (!user) return <Login />; keeps the main JSX flat; changing the key of a component resets its state

chapters.title: Composition, Children and Fragments
points: children is a special prop holding whatever JSX is nested between the opening and closing tags: <Card>content</Card>
Composition beats inheritance: build a generic wrapper such as Card or Layout and pass content in as children
Named slots are plain props that accept JSX: <Layout header={<Nav />} sidebar={<Menu />}>main</Layout>
Fragment <>...</> groups siblings without adding a DOM node; use <Fragment key={id}> when a key is needed in a list
Lifting content up through children avoids prop drilling and prevents re-rendering the passed-in elements when the wrapper's state changes

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: Defining a component inside another component: it is a new type each render, so React remounts it and loses its state
Lowercase component name: <card /> renders as an HTML element, not your component
Calling a component as a function, Card(props), instead of <Card />; this breaks hooks
Forgetting the key, or putting it on the inner element instead of the one returned by map, triggers the warning and bad diffing
Mutating arrays during render (items.sort()) instead of copying first: [...items].sort()

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet
points:
Component: function Name({ a, b, children }) { return
{children}
; }
JSX: one root, close all tags, className and htmlFor, {expr} for JS, style={{}}
List: arr.map(x => <Item key={x.id} {...x} />) with a stable unique id
Conditionals: ternary for either/or, && for show/hide with a boolean (not a number), null for nothing
Composition: <Wrapper>children</Wrapper> or slot props; <>...</> fragment for siblings with no wrapper node
